source_identity.canonical_title: L'homme coupe encore trop souvent la parole à la femme (Manterrupting)

translation.canonical_title: Men still interrupt women far too often (Manterrupting)
translation.displayed_title: Men still interrupt women far too often (Manterrupting)
translation.summary:
Another portmanteau entered the feminist media market in 2015: manterrupting (“man” and “-terrupting,” taken from the English word “interrupting”), describing how men interrupt women and cut them off, most often to correct or contradict them and monopolize the conversation. Jessica Bennett uses it in her book Feminist Fight Club: An Office Survival Manual for a Sexist Workplace. The author defines it as “the unnecessary interruption of a woman by a man.”
Some politicians, such as Donald Trump, have become masters of the practice: he interrupted Hillary Clinton 51 times in 2016 during the presidential debate, compared with 17 interruptions in the other direction. Remnants of a patriarchal culture? Because women entered politics and positions of power more recently, they may therefore have greater difficulty establishing their legitimacy.
For political scientist Frédérique Matonti, the answer comes down to one word: socialization.
Studies of education show that parents, without realizing it, encourage girls to hold back rather than put themselves forward, she explains. Boys are often allowed to make noise, whereas girls must remain discreet and lower their voices. Gradually, children internalize these masculine and feminine values: boys learn to speak up, say they are not afraid and stand their ground, while girls learn to listen and pay attention to others.

source_parameters.name: citation
source_parameters.value: En 1975 déjà, une étude des sociologues Don Zimmerman et Candace West révélait que, lors de 42 conversations entre hommes et femmes, la femme était toujours interrompue. En 2014, une autre étude analysait 900 minutes de conversation homme/femme au sein d’une entreprise. Il s’est avéré que les hommes interrompaient deux fois plus les femmes qu’elles ne le faisaient. En 2015, une autre étude menée sur 12 ans montrait que les femmes travaillant dans le domaine de la justice ne représentaient que 4% des interruptions de parole.

citations.translated_citation: As early as 1975, a study by sociologists Don Zimmerman and Candace West revealed that, in 42 conversations between men and women, the woman was always interrupted. In 2014, another study analyzed 900 minutes of conversation between men and women in a company. It found that men interrupted women twice as often as women interrupted men. In 2015, another study conducted over 12 years showed that women working in the field of justice accounted for only 4% of interruptions.

citations.translated_citation: “Gender constitutes a disadvantage, all other things being equal,” they write. Indeed, in plenary sessions, regardless of the type of intervention (tabling an amendment, raising a point of order, oral questions or explanations of vote), men always speak more than women: over eight sessions between April 2004 and March 2005, men spoke 142 times and women 80 times.
